1: Chapter 1: The Guest on a Rainy Night

It had been raining in Ishikawa for three days straight. Haruka Sato's older sister had left for the capital in the spring, and since then Haruka had been running the town's little pharmacy on her own.
At dusk she shut the storm shutters, tallied the day's sales, blew out the lights, and went up to the second floor.
The moment she lay down, a loud banging on the door came from below, and a man's voice called, “Is anyone there?”
In the doorway stood a drenched young man. Blood seeped from the cloth wrapped around his left arm. He introduced himself as Ken'ichi Mori and said he was a member of the Azure Dragon Society.
“I need my wound tended,” Mori whispered. “I’ll pay. Would three thousand five hundred yen be enough?”
Mori fished a letter wrapped in oil paper from his pocket. “I have to deliver this letter to Seifu by May 18,” he said.
Haruka sighed inwardly. It was herb‑stocking season, and she was so busy she could have used a cat’s paw to help.
Nevertheless, Haruka refused the money and simply said, “I’ll guide you up the mountain early tomorrow morning.”
2: As soon as dawn broke, the two set out. Haruka slung a basket on her back, its contents—rice balls, medicinal herbs, and an old umbrella—packed inside.

On the mid‑slope they met Shigeru Tanaka, an elderly man splitting firewood. He set his axe down and, lowering his voice, said that the previous evening three strangers had been asking around the town’s entrance about a young man who had been injured.
“Haruka, take the back trail,” Tanaka said. “The main road is dangerous.” Haruka bowed in thanks.
The back trail was narrow and slick. Haruka led, placing each foot firmly as she went. Mori followed silently behind.

By noon the rain had stopped, the mountain mist lifted slowly, and the roofs of Seifu appeared in the distance. In front of the gate stood a nun—Shizuka Yamamoto, who tended to visitors at the temple.
Yamamoto received a letter, checked the red seal, and nodded. “The head priest has been waiting for this letter for two years,” she said.
Mori told Haruka, “You saved my life.” She laughed, “Then next time you come, please fix the apothecary’s roof.” Mori stayed at the temple.
At evening Haruka descended the mountain alone. When she reached home it was already dark; she lit a lamp and sat for a long while in the back of the accounting room.
